caption: Figure 1: The surface z = x2 + y2 sliced by the plane y = 1. The red curve is the slice z = x2 + 1; the blue dashed line is its tangent at x = 1. Its slope, fx(1, 1) = 2, is the partial derivative.
Figure 2: One-variable analogue. The tangent line’s rise dy is a linear estimate of the curve’s true rise ∆y; the difference is the error, which shrinks much faster than dx.
Figure 3: A small du × dv rectangle (left) is mapped to a parallelogram spanned by ru du and rv dv (right). Its area is |J| du dv.

Figure 4: Left: restricting f to the line through (a, b) turns the two-variable problem into a one- variable one. Right: the one-variable Taylor polynomials hug the function more tightly as the degree rises — this is why the second-degree terms improve on the linear (tangent-plane) estimate.

Figure 12: A polar “rectangle” of size ∆r × ∆θ is really a wedge of area ≈r ∆r ∆θ — larger r means more area swept per unit ∆θ, which is exactly the factor dA = r dr dθ accounts for.
Figure 1: A × B is perpendicular to the plane containing A and B — direction fixed by the right- hand rule (curl fingers from A to B, thumb gives the result).

Figure 2: Level curves of f(x, y) = x2 + y2 (circles) with ∇f drawn at several points. Every arrow is perpendicular to the circle it sits on, and points toward increasing f (outward, since f grows as you move away from the origin).
Figure 3: The directional derivative is the projection of ∇f onto the chosen direction ˆa — maximal when ˆa aligns with ∇f itself (θ = 0).
Figure 4: Left: F = xi + yj (arrows flow outward everywhere ⇒div F > 0, a source). Right: F = −xi −yj (arrows flow inward ⇒div F < 0, a sink).

Figure 5: Left: F = −yi + xj circulates around the origin — a paddle wheel dropped in would spin, so curl F̸ = 0. Right: a straight, uniform flow like F = j has no local swirl anywhere, so curl F = 0 even though the fluid is clearly moving.

Figure 7: Two neighboring cells circulate in opposite directions along their shared edge, so that contribution cancels exactly. Doing this for every internal edge in the grid leaves only the outer boundary C contributing — the heart of Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’s theorems alike.
Figure 8: At a surface patch dS, only the component of F along the normal ˆn contributes to flux — the rest of F (tangential to the surface) never actually crosses it.

Figure 9: A curved “cap” surface S stretched across the closed curve C. Stokes’ Theorem lets you swap the line integral around C for a surface integral of curl over S — and S can be any surface bounded by C, so pick the easiest one.

Figure 10: Flux out through a closed surface S (arrows) equals the sum of divergence produced at every point enclosed — the Gauss Divergence Theorem, obtained from the same cell-cancellation idea as Green’s Theorem, extended to three dimensions.

Figure 8: Left: Cauchy–Euler solutions against x. Right: the same functions against t = ln x — they become the familiar e2t, e−t, cos t of a constant-coefficient equation. Note that cos(ln x) oscillates infinitely often as x →0+, even though it never repeats on an ordinary axis.
Figure 9: Solutions of (x + 1)2y′′ + (x + 1)y′ −y = 0 are (x + 1)m with m = ±1. The dashed line x = −1 plays the role that x = 0 plays for Cauchy–Euler.
Figure 10: A mass m attached to a wall by a spring (stiffness k) and a damper (coefficient c), driven by an external force F(t).

Figure 11: Three damping regimes, all released from x(0) = 1, x′(0) = 0. Overdamped (c2 > 4mk): slow return, no oscillation. Critically damped (c2 = 4mk): fastest return without overshoot. Underdamped (c2 < 4mk): oscillation inside a decaying envelope.

Figure 13: For z = f(x2 +y2) the level curves are circles. The combination yp−xq = ∇z ·(y, −x) is the rate of change of z along the circles, which is 0: the PDE yp −xq = 0 says “z does not change as you go around the origin”.
Figure 14: The “slope plane”: every point (a, b) on the curve F(p, q) = 0 gives a solution plane z = ax + by + c. Here F = √p + √q −1 and b = (1 −√a)2.

Figure 15: For u = x + 2y, z is constant on each line x + 2y = const. The surface is a “travelling profile” z = f(u) stretched along the lines. This one-variable reduction is what turns the PDE into an ODE.
Figure 16: Both sides of the equation must equal the same separation constant a, which then splits the PDE into two one-variable problems.
Figure 19: The solution u = 6e−3x−2t of ux = 2ut + u with u(x, 0) = 6e−3x: the initial profile (blue) decays uniformly in time, since u is multiplied by e−2t.
